title: African Elephants Often Produce Choruses of Low-Pitched Rumbles. Now, Scientists Are Using A.I. to Decode the Joint Vocalizations
key_facts: A study published 1 Oct 2026 in Scientific Reports used machine learning on 902 recordings of rumbles from wild African savanna elephants in Amboseli National Park, Kenya.
The recordings, made between 1986 and 2022, covered six social contexts such as greetings, contact calls and "let's-go" calls.
The algorithm predicted the elephants' activity from their rumbles better than chance but made many mistakes.
Choruses appear to carry information about who is calling and what they are doing, and sometimes extra fine-grained information.
Individual rumbles became more alike ("vocal convergence") only in cadenced, contact and greeting rumbles; the researchers say more research is needed.
An outside researcher called the findings fascinating but "not really surprising".
quote_evidence: The algorithm predicted the elephants’ activities based on their rumbles better than chance, but it still made plenty of mistakes.
Vocal convergence occurred only during the cadenced, contact and greeting rumbles, so the researchers think it might play some role in helping elephant families coordinate group behaviors.
why_it_matters_hint: Machine learning is being used to test whether group animal calls hold more meaning than single calls.
notes: Quotes from study authors and outside experts are borrowed from Scientific American, New Scientist and Guardian interviews, as the article says.
